title: More Pancreatic Cancer Vaccine Progress - Treatment and Preventative
body_text: Let’s talk about pancreatic cancer vaccines, because there are some really interesting long-running projects in that area. I’ve written several times about a therapeutic vaccine for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (the most common type) being developed by Roche and BioNTech, most recently here. This is the one where they make an individual agent for each patient, based on the neoantigen proteins that their PDAC tumors are producing. The results so far have been encouraging, as that link will show you, with the proviso that the patients in this group were carefully selected - for one thing, they had pancreatic ducal cancer that was suitable for surgery, and not all cases are, generally because they’re been caught too late. The latest update (from April) shows the situation five years after treatment Sixteen patients got this personalized vaccine along with their surgeries, and the initial results were right down the middle: 8 of them showed an immune response after this, and 8 of them didn’t. The five-year results, as you would figure, show that same divide. Of the eight responders, seven of them are still alive. And among the eight nonresponders, only two are. The five-year survival rates for PDAC are all over the place depending on stage when it was diagnosed and its surgical resectibility, but the historical rate (diagnosed 1975 to 2011) without surgery was about 4%, and with surgery about 17%. That latter percentage has been increasing over the years, and for the most favorable situated patients can be as high as 50%, but I’d say that 2-out-of-8 seen here is more typical. But that 7 out of 8 surviving in the responders group? Unheard of. There’s a larger trial going on now at centers around the world, with a larger variety of patients, and it will be very interesting indeed to see what those two key percentages come out as: the percentage of trial participants who respond immunologically, and the percentage of those who survive longer than they otherwise would. Both of these are presumably subject to improvement as we learn more. But most people when they hear the world “vaccine” are thinking of preventatives rather than therapies. Is there a way to vaccinate people at risk of PDAC so that they won’t get cancer in the first place? There are indeed such patients (perhaps 10% of the total) who can be identified by genetic profiling, since there are a number of mutations that increase the risk. We now have a look at just such a vaccine program in this new paper. The team worked with 20 patients with such hereditary PDAC risks and who already showed some sort of lesion/abnormality in the pancreas via radiographic imaging. They received a vaccine targeting six of the most common KRAS mutations (PDAC tumors are among the most RAS-dependent of all cancer types), and there was an immune response in 18 out of the 20, which might well be evidence that the precancerous situation is more open to immunotherapy than after PDAC itself has developed. These patients have now been followed up for two years, and their T-cell responses remain during this time, which is a good sign. So far none of the patients have progressed to outright PDAC, which is also good. Just how good is open to debate, since I’m not sure if there are any good statistics on just how many patients in this category would have progressed to disease otherwise. But there’s reason for optimism: the team did study an unvaccinated control group over this time span, and found that about 7% of them showed reduction or resolution of pancreatic cysts on radiography, while over 37% of the treated group showed the same. That’s certainly pointing in the right direction! It’s early days yet. The cellular responses varied over the 18 individuals, and we don’t know which of these are going to be better in the long run. And as for that long run, no one knows yet if there should be some sort of booster shot or what the optimal timing for it should be. With a lot of immunologic approaches you sort of have to feel your way on these issues. But so far it looks like it could be good news, and I hope that this continues as more patients are studied.
